claim: Bruton's tyrosine kinase (Btk) is a Tec-family tyrosine kinase essential for B-cell function.
source: Bruton's tyrosine kinase (Btk), a Tec-family tyrosine kinase, is essential for B-cell function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about Btk's role in B-cell biology.

claim: Autoinhibited Btk adopts a compact conformation like that of inactive c-Src and c-Abl.
source: Autoinhibited Btk adopts a compact conformation like that of inactive c-Src and c-Abl.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript comparing Btk structure to c-Src and c-Abl structures.

claim: A lipid-binding PH-TH module, unique to Tec kinases, acts in conjunction with the SH2 and SH3 domains to stabilize the inactive conformation of Btk.
source: A lipid-binding PH-TH module, unique to Tec kinases, acts in conjunction with the SH2 and SH3 domains to stabilize the inactive conformation.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure of the PH-TH-kinase construct and biochemical assays showing the role of the PH-TH module in autoinhibition.

claim: Inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), a soluble signaling molecule found in both animal and plant cells, activates Btk.
source: In addition to the expected activation of Btk by membranes containing phosphatidylinositol triphosphate (PIP3), we found that inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), a soluble signaling molecule found in both animal and plant cells, also activates Btk.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical activation assays showing IP6-dependent Btk autophosphorylation and increased catalytic activity.

claim: IP6 activation of Btk is a consequence of transient PH-TH dimerization induced by IP6, which promotes transphosphorylation of the kinase domains.
source: This activation is a consequence of a transient PH-TH dimerization induced by IP6, which promotes transphosphorylation of the kinase domains.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure of IP6-bound PH-TH module showing the Saraste dimer interface and mutagenesis studies disrupting this interface.

claim: Activation by IP6 is unique to Btk among Tec-family kinases based on sequence comparisons.
source: Sequence comparisons with other Tec-family kinases suggest that activation by IP6 is unique to Btk.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment showing that residues critical for IP6 binding at the peripheral site are not conserved in Itk.

claim: Src-family kinases (principally Lyn and Fyn in B-cells, Lck and Fyn in T-cells) are resident at the plasma membrane and respond first to receptor activation.
source: Src-family kinases (principally Lyn and Fyn in B-cells, Lck and Fyn in T-cells), resident at the plasma membrane, respond first to receptor activation.
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge about the signaling cascade in lymphocytes.

claim: Src-family kinases phosphorylate pairs of tyrosine residues in ITAM motifs in the cytoplasmic tails of activated receptors.
source: They phosphorylate pairs of tyrosine residues in ITAM motifs in the cytoplasmic tails of activated receptors (Chu et al., 1998; Mócsai et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010), which in turn recruit the tandem-SH2 domain tyrosine kinases Syk (in B-cells) and ZAP-70 (in T-cells).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Membrane localization of Syk or ZAP-70 leads to the recruitment and activation of Tec-family tyrosine kinases, Btk (in B-cells) and Itk (in T-cells).
source: Membrane localization of Syk or ZAP-70 leads to the recruitment and activation of Tec-family tyrosine kinases, Btk (in B-cells) and Itk (in T-cells) (Andreotti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Btk is present in all hematopoietic cells, except for T-cells and natural killer cells.
source: Btk is present in all hematopoietic cells, except for T-cells and natural killer cells (Tsukada et al., 1993; Lindvall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Btk is part of several receptor-mediated signaling networks, including those initiated by Toll-like receptors, Fc receptors, and G-protein coupled receptors.
source: It is also part of several other receptor-mediated signaling networks, including those initiated by Toll-like receptors (Jefferies et al., 2003), Fc receptors (Kawakami et al., 1994), and G-protein coupled receptors (Tsukada et al., 1994; Bence et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Btk is critical for the generation of calcium flux in response to receptor activation because it activates phospholipase C-γ2 (PLC-γ2).
source: Btk is critical for the generation of calcium flux in response to receptor activation, because it activates phospholipase C-γ2 (PLC-γ2), which produces the second messengers diaceylglycerol (DAG) and inositol (1,4,5)-trisphosphate (IP3).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Btk's role in signaling.

claim: Btk dysfunction is the cause of X-linked agammaglobulinemia, a severe disease of primary immunodeficiency.
source: Btk dysfunction is the cause of X-linked agammaglobulinemia, a severe disease of primary immunodeficiency (Tsukada et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The Tec family kinases have a lipid-interaction module attached to the N terminus of a Src-like module (i.e., concatenation of an SH3 domain, an SH2 domain and a tyrosine kinase domain).
source: The Tec family kinases have a lipid-interaction module attached to the N terminus of a Src-like module (i.e., concatenation of an SH3 domain, an SH2 domain and a tyrosine kinase domain) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the domain architecture diagram in Figure 1A and is established knowledge about Tec kinase structure.

claim: Like the non-receptor tyrosine kinase c-Abl, the Tec kinases lack a C-terminal tyrosine phosphorylation site that in Src kinases engages the SH2 domain in an autoinhibitory interaction.
source: Like the non-receptor tyrosine kinase c-Abl, the Tec kinases lack a C-terminal tyrosine phosphorylation site that in Src kinases engages the SH2 domain in an autoinhibitory interaction (Sicheri et al., 1997; Xu et al., 1997; Nagar et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies of c-Abl and Src kinases.

claim: The lipid-interaction module of the Tec kinases is an extended plekstrin homology (PH) domain fused to a Tec homology (TH) domain.
source: The lipid-interaction module of the Tec kinases is an extended plekstrin homology (PH) domain fused to a Tec homology (TH) domain (Hyvönen and Saraste, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The PH-TH binds PIP3 in membranes, or the soluble head group of PIP3, inositol tetrakisphosphate (IP4), in solution.
source: The PH-TH binds PIP3 in membranes, or the soluble head group of PIP3, inositol tetrakisphosphate (IP4), in solution.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PH-TH module binding properties.

claim: A flexible linker connects the PH-TH module to the Src-like module; its length varies from 26 residues in Itk to 45 residues in Btk.
source: A flexible linker connects the PH-TH module to the Src-like module; its length varies from 26 residues in Itk, the Tec family kinase in T-cells, to 45 residues in Btk.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of Tec family kinases.

claim: B-cell activation leads to rapid phosphorylation of Tyr 551 in the kinase domain and Tyr 223 in the SH3 domain of Btk.
source: B-cell activation leads to rapid phosphorylation of Tyr 551 in the kinase domain and Tyr 223 in the SH3 domain of Btk (Park et al., 1996; Rawlings et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of Tyr 551 increases Btk catalytic activity.
source: Tyr 551 corresponds to the canonical phosphorylation site in the activation loop of tyrosine kinases; as expected, its phosphorylation increases Btk catalytic activity (Rawlings et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of Tyr 223 has been reported to have no apparent influence on Btk catalytic activity.
source: Phosphorylation of Tyr 223 has been reported to have no apparent influence on Btk catalytic activity (Park et al., 1996; Middendorp et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tyr 223 lies within the peptide-binding groove of the SH3 domain, and its phosphorylation alters SH3 domain selectivity among binding partners.
source: It lies within the peptide-binding groove of the SH3 domain, and its phosphorylation alters SH3 domain selectivity among binding partners (Morrogh et al., 1999; Middendorp et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Binding of a Tec-kinase PH domain to the membrane lipid PIP3 provides a control mechanism for switching on the kinase through membrane recruitment that triggers trans-autophosphorylation.
source: Binding of a Tec-kinase PH domain to the membrane lipid PIP3, produced as a consequence of receptor activation, provides a simple control mechanism for switching on the kinase. Membrane recruitment triggers trans-autophosphorylation, through increased local concentration, or trans-phosphorylation by membrane-bound Src-family kinases, thereby activating the Tec kinase (Rawlings et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and represents the established model for Btk activation.

claim: The structure of the Src-like module of Btk is in an assembled and inactive conformation, resembling those of inactive c-Abl and of the Src kinases c-Src and Hck.
source: One structure is of the Src-like module, in an assembled and inactive conformation, resembling those of inactive c-Abl and of the Src kinases c-Src and Hck (Sicheri et al., 1997; Xu et al., 1997; Nagar et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure determination and comparison to cited structures.

claim: The PH-TH module stabilizes the inactive conformation of the kinase by interacting with the N lobe.
source: We find that the PH-TH module stabilizes the inactive conformation of the kinase by interacting with the N lobe.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure of the PH-TH-kinase construct showing the interface.

claim: The inactive conformation of Btk is a compact one, in which the PH-TH module cooperates with the SH2 and SH3 domains to maintain an inactive structure.
source: The inactive conformation of Btk is thus a compact one, in which the PH-TH module cooperates with the SH2 and SH3 domains to maintain an inactive structure.
evidence: This is supported by the composite model combining the two crystal structures and molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: IP6 is a soluble signaling molecule ubiquitous in animal and plant cells.
source: We also report a set of findings that reveal an unanticipated role for the PH-TH module in activating the kinase domain. We find that inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), a soluble signaling molecule ubiquitous in animal and plant cells (Szwergold et al., 1987; Vallejo et al., 1987), can activate Btk strongly.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A previously undetected binding site on the PH-TH module, distinct from the canonical PIP3/IP4 site, is critical for activation by IP6.
source: We have determined a crystal structure of the PH-TH module of Btk bound to IP6 and identified a previously undetected binding site on the PH-TH module, distinct from the canonical PIP3/IP4 site. The new site is critical for activation by IP6.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure of IP6-bound PH-TH module and mutagenesis studies.

claim: The possibility that PH dimerization might be important for Btk activation was first proposed by Saraste and colleagues.
source: The possibility that PH dimerization might be important for Btk activation was first proposed by Saraste and colleagues (Hyvönen and Saraste, 1997), and we now show that the dimer interface identified previously is essential for IP6-dependent Btk activation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and the current mutagenesis data.

claim: IP6-triggered transient dimerization of the PH domain may provide a membrane-independent mechanism for activating Btk in the nucleus or cytoplasm or may have a role in feedback stimulation of Btk that has been activated by PIP3 at the membrane.
source: IP6-triggered transient dimerization of the PH domain may provide a membrane-independent mechanism for activating Btk in the nucleus or cytoplasm or may have a role in feedback stimulation of Btk that has been activated by PIP3 at the membrane.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings.

claim: The structure of the SH3 domain of Btk is nearly identical to those determined previously using NMR (the r.m.s. deviation for 53 Cα atoms is 0.9 Å).
source: The structure of the SH3 domain of Btk is nearly identical to those determined previously using NMR (the r.m.s. deviation for 53 Cα atoms is 0.9 Å) (Hansson et al., 1998; Tzeng et al., 2000), except for the expected differences seen at the N and C termini.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited NMR structures.

claim: The conserved features of the SH3/linker interaction in Btk include the polyproline type-II helix conformation adopted by residues 383–387 in the SH2-kinase linker, including the proline at position 385, and the overall hydrophobic character of the peptide-binding pocket on the SH3 domain.
source: When compared with the other autoinhibited SH3-SH2-kinase structures (c-Src, Hck, c-Abl), the conserved features of the SH3/linker interaction in Btk are the polyproline type-II helix conformation adopted by residues 383–387 in the SH2-kinase linker, including the proline at position 385, and the overall hydrophobic character of the peptide-binding pocket on the SH3 domain (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and comparison to other kinase structures.

claim: Binding of exogenous protein ligands to the Btk SH3 domain would disassemble the Src-like inactive conformation, as seen for the Src family kinase Hck.
source: Binding of exogenous protein ligands to the Btk SH3 domain would disassemble the Src-like inactive conformation, as seen for the Src family kinase Hck (Moarefi et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an inference based on analogy to Hck, supported by citation.

claim: The SH2 domain of Btk has a marginally stable internal structure, as shown by the domain swap.
source: The domain itself has a marginally stable internal structure, as shown by the domain swap, and it is probably imperfectly locked in place.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of domain swapping in the crystal structure.

claim: The domain swap in the Btk SH2 domain occurs in the same location within the SH2 domain as a domain swap seen in a Grb2 SH2-domain crystal structure.
source: The domain swap occurs in the same location within the SH2 domain as a domain swap seen in a Grb2 SH2-domain crystal structure (Schiering et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to the cited Grb2 structure.

claim: The exchange in the domain-swapped SH2 occurs such that helix B of one polypeptide chain packs against the main β-sheet of the other and vice versa.
source: The SH2 domain opens up at a position within the subsidiary β-sheet, so that helix B of one polypeptide chain packs against the main β-sheet of the other and vice versa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The domain swap occurs in solution for Btk, as only the dimeric species crystallizes.
source: This exchange occurs in solution for Btk, as only the dimeric species crystallizes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only the dimeric form was obtained in crystals.

claim: There is no evidence that a domain-swapped dimer (or, indeed, any stable dimer) is a functional state of intact Btk.
source: There is no evidence that a domain-swapped dimer (or, indeed, any stable dimer) is a functional state of intact Btk, and so it is likely that the assembled state involves a single polypeptide chain, rather than two inter-folded chains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of evidence for functional dimers.

claim: The unphosphorylated activation loop of Btk folds into the mouth of the catalytic cleft, blocking part of the substrate-binding site.
source: The unphosphorylated activation loop of Btk folds into the mouth of the catalytic cleft, blocking part of the substrate-binding site, and helix αC lies at the margin of the N lobe, preventing formation of a Glu-Lys salt bridge conserved in all catalytically active protein kinases (Taylor and Kornev, 2011) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The activation loop of Btk is in a conformation seen in the structure of a Btk kinase domain-inhibitor complex and in autoinhibited c-Src.
source: The activation loop of Btk is in a conformation seen in the structure of a Btk kinase domain-inhibitor complex (PDB: 3OCS; [Di Paolo et al., 2011]), and in autoinhibited c-Src (the r.m.s. deviation from c-Src is 2.3 Å for the 24 α-carbons of the activation loop), but the cleft between the two lobes of the kinase is substantially more open in Btk than in c-Src.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited structures.

claim: A network of polar interactions present in the autoinhibited forms of c-Src and Hck is also present in the Btk conformation in the crystals.
source: A network of polar interactions present in the autoinhibited forms of c-Src and Hck is also present in the Btk conformation in our crystals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data and comparison to c-Src and Hck.

claim: Activation of Btk entails a shuffling of salt-bridge and polar hydrogen-bond partners, described in the case of Src kinases as an 'electrostatic switch'.
source: Activation thus entails a shuffling of salt-bridge and polar hydrogen-bond partners, described in the case of Src kinases as an 'electrostatic switch' (Ozkirimli and Post, 2006; Banavali and Roux, 2009) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison to Src kinases and supported by citations.

claim: The inactive conformation of Btk is stabilized by interactions made by the SH2-kinase linker, with Leu 390 of the linker sandwiched between residues Trp 421 and Tyr 461 in the kinase domain.
source: In addition, the inactive conformation is stabilized by interactions made by the SH2-kinase linker. Leu 390 of the linker (corresponding to Trp 260 in c-Src) is sandwiched between residues Trp 421 and Tyr 461 in the kinase domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The hydrophobic packing between Trp 421 and Leu 390 would not be possible in the active conformation of the kinase domain.
source: The hydrophobic packing between Trp 421 and Leu 390 would not be possible in the active conformation of the kinase domain.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison to the modeled active conformation.

claim: The PH-TH module contacts the kinase N lobe in the PH-TH-kinase structure.
source: The PH-TH module contacts the kinase N lobe.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure of the PH-TH-kinase construct.

claim: The interface between PH-TH and kinase in Btk differs substantially from the one found in Akt1.
source: The interface differs substantially from the one found in Akt1, another PH-domain regulated kinase (Wu et al., 2010) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to the cited Akt1 structure.

claim: In Akt1, the PH domain sits in front of the catalytic cleft of the kinase, blocking peptide substrate binding.
source: In Akt1, the PH domain sits in front of the catalytic cleft of the kinase, blocking peptide substrate binding.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Akt1 structure.

claim: In Btk, the PH-kinase interface does not directly occlude the active site.
source: In Btk, the PH-kinase interface does not directly occlude the active site.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure of the PH-TH-kinase construct.

claim: Tyr 134 at the C terminus of helix α2 of the PH-TH packs into a groove between Trp 395 at the linker-kinase junction and helix αC in the kinase N lobe.
source: In particular, Tyr 134 at the C terminus of helix α2 of the PH-TH packs into a groove between Trp 395 at the linker-kinase junction and helix αC in the kinase N lobe.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The PH-TH/kinase interactions are expected to stabilize the inactive conformation of the kinase by hindering the shift in helix αC that accompanies kinase activation.
source: We expect these interactions to stabilize the inactive conformation of the kinase, by hindering the shift in helix αC that accompanies kinase activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations of the SH3-SH2-kinase module showed that the initial and final conformations of the SH3 and kinase domains had r.m.s. deviations in Cα positions of only ∼3.0 and ∼2.0 Å, respectively.
source: In simulations of the SH3-SH2-kinase module, the initial and final conformations of the SH3 and kinase domains had r.m.s. deviations in Cα positions of only ∼3.0 and ∼2.0 Å, respectively, after first aligning the C lobe of the kinase domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: In simulations of the SH3-SH2-kinase module, the SH2 domain shifted by ∼6 Å, with a roughly 10° rotation that brought it closer to the C lobe of the kinase domain.
source: The SH2 domain shifted by ∼6 Å, with a roughly 10° rotation that brought it closer to the C lobe of the kinase domain and closer to its position in the inactive forms of c-Src, Hck, and c-Abl.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: In simulations of the PH-TH-kinase construct, the interface with the kinase domain remained intact, but the PH-TH module wobbled back and forth through a rotation of about 20°.
source: In simulations of the PH-TH-kinase construct, the interface with the kinase domain remained intact, but the PH-TH module wobbled back and forth through a rotation of about 20° (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The PH-TH module pivots about an apparent anchor point at the C terminus of helix α2, at the center of the autoinhibitory contact.
source: The PH-TH module pivots about an apparent anchor point at the C terminus of helix α2, at the center of the autoinhibitory contact (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The kinase domain of Btk has low catalytic activity and autophosphorylates very slowly, like the c-Abl kinase domain and unlike those of the Src family.
source: The kinase domain of Btk has low catalytic activity and autophosphorylates very slowly, like the c-Abl kinase domain and unlike those of the Src family (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: There is no detectable change over 90 min in the level of phosphorylation of the Btk kinase domain at 4 μM concentration.
source: For example, there is no detectable change over 90 min in the level of phosphorylation of the Btk kinase domain at 4 μM concentration.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: Inclusion of the SH2 domain and the SH2-kinase linker (but not the SH3 domain or the PH-TH module) increases Btk autophosphorylation substantially.
source: Inclusion of the SH2 domain and the SH2-kinase linker (but not the SH3 domain or the PH-TH module) increases Btk autophosphorylation substantially (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data comparing different constructs.

claim: In c-Abl, the SH2 domain docks onto the N lobe of the kinase domain and stabilizes the active conformation.
source: We have not studied how the SH2 domain increases activity, but we note that in c-Abl, the SH2 domain docks onto the N lobe of the kinase domain and stabilizes the active conformation and that activation by the SH2 domain is also seen in Csk (Sondhi and Cole, 1999) and c-Fes (Nagar et al., 2006; Filippakopoulos et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The autoactivation rate of the complete Src-like module of Btk is lower than that of the SH2-kinase module.
source: The autoactivation rate of the complete Src-like module of Btk is lower than that of the SH2-kinase module (Figure 4B), as expected from the joint clamping effect of the SH3 and SH2 domains.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: The autoactivation rates of Y223A and Y268A mutants are about sixfold greater than that of the unmutated enzyme and comparable to that of the SH2-kinase module.
source: The autoactivation rates of both mutants are indeed about sixfold greater than that of the unmutated enzyme and comparable to that of the SH2-kinase module (the rate of activation is estimated from the slope of activity vs time, and is only a rough measure because of non-linearity; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: Phosphorylation of Tyr 89 in the SH3-kinase interface is necessary for full activation of c-Abl.
source: An analogous interaction regulates c-Abl activation: phosphorylation of Tyr 89, in the SH3-kinase interface, is necessary for full activation (Brasher and Van Etten, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mutations expected to disrupt the PH-TH-kinase interface increase the autoactivation rate of full-length Btk.
source: Mutations expected to disrupt the PH-TH-kinase interface likewise increase the autoactivation rate of full-length Btk, consistent with our inferences from examining the interface between the PH-TH and the kinase N lobe (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: Removal of the entire PH-TH module, while retaining the Src-like regulatory components, increases the rate of autoactivation about threefold.
source: Removal of the entire PH-TH module, while retaining the Src-like regulatory components, increases the rate of autoactivation about threefold, as estimated from the slopes of the activity curves in Figure 4.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: SUVs containing 75% DOPC, 20% DOPS, and 5% PIP3 produce a rapid and substantial activation of Btk.
source: SUVs containing 75% DOPC, 20% DOPS, and 5% PIP3 produce a rapid and substantial activation of Btk (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: At a Btk concentration of 2 μM, robust phosphorylation can be detected within the first 5 min of reaction in the presence of PIP3-containing vesicles.
source: At a Btk concentration of 2 μM, robust phosphorylation can be detected within the first 5 min of reaction in the presence of these vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: The extent of activation depends on the concentration of PIP3 in the vesicles, presumably because increasing the PIP3 fraction increases the surface density of Btk on the lipid vesicles and thereby increases the rate of trans-autophosphorylation.
source: The extent of activation depends on the concentration of PIP3 in the vesicles, presumably because increasing the PIP3 fraction increases the surface density of Btk on the lipid vesicles and thereby increases the rate of trans-autophosphorylation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data and is a reasonable inference.

claim: The local concentration of Btk on the vesicle surface is in the millimolar range, that is, 100-fold greater than in bulk solution.
source: An estimate of the surface density of PIP3 on these vesicles suggests that the local concentration of Btk on the vesicle surface is in the millimolar range, that is, 100-fold greater than in bulk solution (see 'Materials and methods' for detailed calculations).
evidence: This is based on calculations described in the methods section.

claim: IP4 itself has no effect on the rate of Btk activation in solution.
source: IP4 itself has no effect on the rate of Btk activation in solution, demonstrating that the role of PIP3 is to recruit Btk to the membrane without necessarily triggering an allosteric effect.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: IP6 promotes Btk autophosphorylation strongly at 2 μM protein concentration, substantially enhancing Btk catalytic activity within the first 5 min after addition.
source: Quite unexpectedly, we discovered that inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) promotes Btk autophosphorylation strongly at 2 μM protein concentration, substantially enhancing Btk catalytic activity within the first 5 min after addition (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: Certain inositol pentakisphosphates (IP5) produce a milder activation than IP6, but these required higher protein concentration and longer times for appreciable autophosphorylation.
source: We also saw a milder activation with certain inositol pentakisphosphates (IP5), but these required higher protein concentration and longer times for appreciable autophosphorylation than did IP6 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: The EC50 value for IP6 activation is around 20 μM, in the range of the physiological concentration of IP6 in cells, which is 10 μM–80 μM.
source: The EC50 value for IP6 activation is around 20 μM (Figure 5D), in the range of the physiological concentration of IP6 in cells, which is 10 μM–80 μM (Irvine and Schell, 2001; Shears, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data and citations to prior literature on IP6 concentrations.

claim: In the presence of a saturating concentration of IP6 (100 μM), full-length Btk is activated within the first 5 min of reaction time.
source: In the presence of a saturating concentration of IP6 (100 μM), full-length Btk is activated within the first 5 min of reaction time, in contrast to the 30 min and 120 min that are required for the activation of the SH2-kinase module and full-length Btk, respectively, in the absence of IP6 or PIP3-containing vesicles (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: Once fully activated, the catalytic rates of various Btk constructs are the same with or without IP6 addition, suggesting that the effect of IP6 is to change the rate of autophosphorylation, and that it does not affect the catalytic machinery directly.
source: Once fully activated, the catalytic rates of various Btk constructs are the same with or without IP6 addition, suggesting that the effect of IP6 is to change the rate of autophosphorylation, and that it does not affect the catalytic machinery directly (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data and is a reasonable inference.

claim: Activation by IP6 required only the PH-TH module and not the SH3 and SH2 domains.
source: By comparing constructs, we determined which domains in Btk are responsible for the IP6 response. Activation by IP6 required only the PH-TH module and not the SH3 and SH2 domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data comparing different constructs.

claim: A PH-TH-kinase construct that contained the PH-TH-SH3 linker and the SH2-kinase linker (with a total linker length of 45 residues) had the same response to IP6 as did full-length Btk.
source: A PH-TH-kinase construct that contained the PH-TH-SH3 linker and the SH2-kinase linker (with a total linker length of 45 residues) had the same response to IP6 as did full-length Btk (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: The shortest linker necessary for activation by IP6 contained only 13 residues from the SH2-kinase linker.
source: The shortest linker necessary for activation contained only 13 residues from the SH2-kinase linker; we used this construct to determine the crystal structure described earlier (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: The catalytic activity of the fully activated PH-TH-kinase construct was about threefold lower than that of full-length Btk, which can be explained by the absence of the SH2 domain.
source: The catalytic activity of the fully activated PH-TH-kinase construct was about threefold lower than that of full-length Btk. This lower activity can be explained by the absence of the SH2 domain.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data and is a reasonable inference.

claim: IP6 has no effect on activation of the isolated kinase domain of Btk, suggesting that it is not a direct allosteric activator of the enzyme.
source: IP6 has no effect on activation of the isolated kinase domain of Btk, suggesting that it is not a direct allosteric activator of the enzyme.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data and is a reasonable inference.

claim: The protein kinase CK2 is activated by IP6, which binds to the kinase domain and dislodges an inhibitory interaction between CK2 and the protein Nopp140.
source: The protein kinase CK2 is activated by IP6, which binds to the kinase domain and dislodges an inhibitory interaction between CK2 and the protein Nopp140 (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The IP4-binding site on the PH-TH module (the 'canonical binding site') is located ∼15 Å from the kinase-interacting surface of the PH-TH module.
source: The IP4-binding site on the PH-TH module (the 'canonical binding site') is located ∼15 Å from the kinase-interacting surface of the PH-TH module (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The structure of the PH-TH-kinase construct, in which no inositol phosphates are bound, resembles closely that of the liganded PH domain in the vicinity of the PH-kinase interface.
source: The structure of the PH-TH-kinase construct, in which no inositol phosphates are bound, resembles closely that of the liganded PH domain (Baraldi et al., 1999) in the vicinity of the PH-kinase interface, consistent with the failure of IP4 to activate Btk.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to the cited structure and biochemical data.

claim: Among the four domains in Btk, only the PH-TH module interacts with IP6 as shown by ITC measurements.
source: The ITC measurements show that among the four domains in Btk, only the PH-TH module interacts with IP6.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data.

claim: At 150 mM NaCl concentration, the titration curve for IP6 binding to the PH-TH module can be fit by a one-site model for binding, with a dissociation constant, Kd, of 250 nM.
source: At 150 mM NaCl concentration, the titration curve for IP6 binding to the PH-TH module can be fit by a one-site model for binding, with a dissociation constant, Kd, of 250 nM (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data.

claim: Arg 28 and Asn 24 have been shown previously to be critical for IP4 binding.
source: Arg 28 and Asn 24 have been shown previously to be critical for IP4 binding (Hyvönen and Saraste, 1997; Baraldi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IP4 binds to the PH-TH module with a Kd value of 30 nM, and the R28C/N24E mutation in the PH-TH module reduces IP4 binding to an undetectable level.
source: IP4 binds to the PH-TH module with a Kd value of 30 nM, and the R28C/N24E mutation in the PH-TH module reduces IP4 binding to an undetectable level (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data.

claim: The ITC signal of IP6 binding to the R28C/N24E mutant is reduced greatly but not completely abolished, and the residual signal corresponds to a dissociation constant between 5 μM and 10 μM.
source: The ITC signal of IP6 binding to the R28C/N24E mutant is reduced greatly but not completely abolished, and the residual signal corresponds to a dissociation constant between 5 μM and 10 μM.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data.

claim: The residual binding of IP6 to the IP4-binding deficient mutant is relatively weak, but the observed affinity is consistent with the EC50 value of 20 μM for IP6 activation.
source: Although the residual binding of IP6 to the IP4-binding deficient mutant is relatively weak, the observed affinity is consistent with the EC50 value of 20 μM for IP6 activation, as determined in our activation assays (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an inference connecting ITC and activation assay data.

claim: No significant activation was observed when the IP6 concentration was lower than 5 μM, a level still high enough to saturate the canonical binding site.
source: We observed no significant activation when the IP6 concentration was lower than 5 μM, a level still high enough to saturate the canonical binding site.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: The R28C/N24E mutant that is deficient in IP4 binding remains highly responsive to IP6 stimulation, with only a slight reduction in the activation kinetics as compared to the wild-type protein.
source: We also found that the R28C/N24E mutant that is deficient in IP4 binding remains highly responsive to IP6 stimulation, with only a slight reduction in the activation kinetics as compared to the wild-type protein (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: The canonical binding site of the PH-TH module may not play a major role in the IP6-mediated activation of Btk.
source: These observations imply that the canonical binding site of the PH-TH module may not play a major role in the IP6-mediated activation of Btk.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutagenesis and binding data.

claim: There are four PH-TH modules in the asymmetric unit of the IP6-bound crystal, which form two dimers, similar to those seen in other structures of the Btk PH-TH module.
source: There are four PH-TH modules in the asymmetric unit of the crystal, which form two dimers, similar to those seen in other structures of the Btk PH-TH module (Figure 7D) (Hyvönen and Saraste, 1997; Baraldi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data and comparison to cited structures.

claim: The only structural changes in the IP6-bound PH-TH module, relative to the apo- or IP4-bound PH-TH module, are in the loop regions.
source: The only structural changes in the IP6-bound PH-TH module, relative to the apo- or IP4-bound PH-TH module, are in the loop regions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of crystal structures.

claim: The four PH-TH modules in the asymmetric unit have six bound IP6 molecules, each with clearly resolved electron density.
source: The four PH-TH modules in the asymmetric unit have six bound IP6 molecules, each with clearly resolved electron density.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Four of the IP6 molecules are in the canonical binding sites on each module.
source: Four of the IP6 molecules are in the canonical binding sites on each module.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: At the canonical sites, residues Asn 24, Tyr 39, Arg 28, and Lys 12 coordinate phosphate groups on the 2, 3, and 4 positions of the myo-inositol ring; these are also the key residues involved in IP4 binding.
source: At those sites, residues Asn 24, Tyr 39, Arg 28, and Lys 12 coordinate phosphate groups on the 2, 3, and 4 positions of the myo-inositol ring; these are also the key residues involved in IP4 binding (Baraldi et al., 1999) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data and comparison to cited structure.

claim: The loop between strands β1 and β2, which is important for IP4 binding, is largely disordered in the IP6-bound structure.
source: The loop between strands β1 and β2, which is important for IP4 binding, is largely disordered in our structure (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: There are fewer interactions at the canonical site between the PH-TH module and IP6 than seen for IP4, consistent with the relative affinities of the two ligands.
source: There are fewer interactions at the canonical site between the PH-TH module and IP6 than seen for IP4, consistent with the relative affinities of the two ligands (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of crystal structures and ITC data.

claim: The two other IP6 molecules in the crystallographic asymmetric unit are bound at a peripheral site on the surface formed by an elongated β hairpin involving strands β3 and β4 of each PH-TH module.
source: The two other IP6 molecules in the crystallographic asymmetric unit are bound at a peripheral site. This site is on the surface formed by an elongated β hairpin involving strands β3 and β4 of each PH-TH module.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The peripheral IP6 binding site has not been seen in any other PH domain; it differs from the two well-characterized lipid-binding sites in the PH domains of Pleckstrin and β-spectrin.
source: This site has not been seen in any other PH domain (Lemmon, 2008); it differs from the two well-characterized lipid-binding sites in the PH domains of Pleckstrin (Ferguson et al., 1995) and β-spectrin (Hyvönen et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited structures and a review.

claim: As in the canonical binding site, interactions between IP6 and the peripheral site are predominantly electrostatistic.
source: As in the canonical binding site, interactions between IP6 and the peripheral site are predominantly electrostatistic (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Unlike the canonical site, which has a well-defined groove within which the inositol phosphates are bound, the peripheral site is relatively flat.
source: Unlike the canonical site, which has a well-defined groove within which the inositol phosphates are bound, the peripheral site is relatively flat (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: IP6 bound at the peripheral site is sandwiched between two PH-TH modules, interacting with the peripheral sites on both.
source: A feature of the crystallographic lattice is that IP6 bound at the peripheral site is sandwiched between two PH-TH modules, interacting with the peripheral sites on both (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Residues Arg 49, Lys 52, Lys 36, and Tyr 40 at the peripheral binding site of one subunit coordinate phosphate groups at the 1, 2, 3, and 4 positions of the myo-inositol ring.
source: Residues Arg 49, Lys 52, Lys 36, and Tyr 40 at the peripheral binding site of one subunit (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) coordinate phosphate groups at the 1, 2, 3, and 4 positions of the myo-inositol ring.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: A subset of residues, Lys 52 and Lys 36, on the other PH-TH module interact from the opposite side of the myo-inositol ring with the phosphate group at position 3.
source: A subset of these residues, Lys 52 and Lys 36, on the other PH-TH module interact from the opposite side of the myo-inositol ring with the phosphate group at position 3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The bridging interactions provided by IP6 generate an open-ended chain of PH-TH dimers in the crystal lattice.
source: The bridging interactions provided by IP6 generate an open-ended chain of PH-TH dimers in the crystal lattice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Based on the limited interactions across the crystallographic interface forming the open-ended chain, this chain is not believed to be relevant to the function of Btk.
source: Based on the limited interactions across this crystallographic interface, we do not believe that this open-ended chain is relevant to the function of Btk.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: A Btk variant with mutations R49S and K52S in the peripheral binding site autophosphorylates slowly and has very little response to IP6.
source: We mutated Arg 49 and Lys 52, in the peripheral binding site of the PH-TH module, to serine in full-length Btk. This Btk variant autophosphorylates slowly, as does wild-type Btk, and it has very little response to IP6 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: No detectable binding was seen when IP6 was added to a PH-TH module with mutations at both the canonical and the peripheral sites in ITC experiments.
source: In ITC experiments, we saw no detectable binding when we added IP6 to a PH-TH module with mutations at both the canonical and the peripheral sites, further confirming that the residual binding of IP6 to the IP4-binding deficient mutant is at the peripheral binding site (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data.

claim: The disposition of the IP6 molecule can be determined unambiguously from the electron density because the phosphate group at the 2 position juts out from the plane of the myo-inositol ring.
source: The disposition of the IP6 molecule can be determined unambiguously from the electron density because the phosphate group at the 2 position juts out from the plane of the myo-inositol ring (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: IP6 at the peripheral binding site interacts with the primary PH-TH module to which it is bound through the phosphates at positions 1, 2, 3, and 4.
source: IP6 at the peripheral binding site interacts with the primary PH-TH module to which it is bound through the phosphates at positions 1, 2, 3, and 4.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: None of the inositol phosphates used in the experiments, other than IP6, can fully satisfy the criterion of interacting through phosphates at positions 1, 2, 3, and 4, which may underlie the specificity of the PH-TH module for IP6.
source: None of the inositol phosphates used in our experiments, other than IP6, can fully satisfy this criterion, which may underlie the specificity of the PH-TH module for IP6.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and biochemical data.

claim: Two isomers of IP5, I(2,3,4,5,6)P5 and I(1,2,3,5,6)P5, have a mildly activating effect on Btk; they are more effective than I(1,3,4,5,6)P5.
source: Two isomers of IP5, I(2,3,4,5,6)P5 and I(1,2,3,5,6)P5, have a mildly activating effect on Btk; they are more effective than I(1,3,4,5,6)P5.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: These comparisons indicate an important role in Btk activation for the phosphate at position 2 of the inositol ring.
source: These comparisons indicate an important role in Btk activation for the phosphate at position 2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference based on biochemical assay data.

claim: In the cell, the only known enzyme that can add a phosphate to the hydroxyl group at position 2 of a myo-inositol ring is inositol 1,3,4,5,6-pentakisphosphate 2-kinase, which produces IP6.
source: In the cell, the only known enzyme that can add a phosphate to the hydroxyl group at position 2 of a myo-inositol ring is inositol 1,3,4,5,6-pentakisphosphate 2-kinase (York et al., 1999), which produces IP6.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: IP6, and inositol pyrophosphates, such as IP7 and IP8, may be the only cellular phosphates that can interact with the peripheral site in the Btk PH-TH module.
source: As a consequence, IP6, and inositol pyrophosphates, such as IP7 and IP8, may be the only cellular phosphates that can interact with the peripheral site in the Btk PH-TH module.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural requirements and knowledge of cellular inositol phosphate metabolism.

claim: Strong activation of Btk by concentration on PIP3-containing membranes suggests that IP6 might promote dimerization or oligomerization of Btk in solution.
source: Strong activation of Btk by concentration on PIP3-containing membranes suggests that IP6 might promote dimerization or oligomerization of Btk in solution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the membrane activation data.

claim: Neither multi-angle light scattering nor size exclusion chromatography gave convincing evidence for IP6-induced association, at Btk concentrations up to 30 μM.
source: Neither multi-angle light scattering nor size exclusion chromatography gave convincing evidence for IP6-induced association, at Btk concentrations up to 30 μM.
evidence: This is supported by biophysical characterization data.

claim: In every crystal structure of the Btk PH-TH module, as well as in the structure of the PH-TH-kinase construct, the module forms very similar crystallographic dimers.
source: Nevertheless, we found it striking that in every crystal structure of the Btk PH-TH module, as well as in our structure of the PH-TH-kinase construct, the module forms very similar crystallographic dimers (Figure 7D) (PDB entry: 1BTK [Hyvönen and Saraste, 1997]; PDB entry:1B55 and 1BWN [Baraldi et al., 1999]; see also PDB entry: 2Z0P).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of multiple crystal structures.

claim: The Saraste dimer is formed by symmetric interactions between helix α1 and strands β3 and β4 of the PH-TH module.
source: The Saraste dimer is formed by symmetric interactions between helix α1 and strands β3 and β4 of the PH-TH module (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The largely hydrophobic dimer interface has a buried surface area of ∼1000 Å2 on each molecule.
source: The largely hydrophobic dimer interface has a buried surface area of ∼1000 Å2 on each molecule.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Phe 44 and Tyr 42 on strand β3, Ile 9 on strand β1 and IIe 95 on helix α1 create a hydrophobic patch in one subunit of the dimer that packs tightly against the corresponding patch on the other subunit.
source: Phe 44 and Tyr 42 on strand β3, Ile 9 on strand β1 and IIe 95 on helix α1 create a hydrophobic patch in one subunit of the dimer that packs tightly against the corresponding patch on the other subunit (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Three mutants in which hydrophobic residues at the Saraste dimer interface were replaced with arginines showed little or no response to IP6.
source: To test whether the Saraste dimer interface is important for IP6-mediated Btk activation, we made three mutants in which we replaced hydrophobic residues at the Saraste dimer interface with arginines and compared their autophosphorylation rates and their response to IP6 with those of wild-type Btk. All three sets of mutant proteins showed little or no response to IP6 (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: The Saraste dimer interface mutations do not affect the autophosphorylation rate of Btk in the absence of IP6.
source: These mutations do not affect the autophosphorylation rate of Btk in the absence of IP6.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: The Saraste dimer interface promotes Btk association in the presence of IP6.
source: We conclude that the Saraste dimer interface promotes Btk association in the presence of IP6.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutagenesis data.

claim: The activation of Class I Histone Deacetylases (HDACs) requires the formation of a multi-subunit co-repressor complex, in which Ins(1,4,5,6)P4 serves as an intermolecular glue that cements the complex together.
source: The activation of Class I Histone Deacetylases (HDACs) requires the formation of a multi-subunit co-repressor complex, in which Ins(1,4,5,6)P4 serves as an intermolecular glue that cements the complex together (Watson et al., 2012; Millard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mechanism of IP6-induced transient Btk dimerization is fundamentally different from HDAC activation, in that the peripheral IP6 binding site is just outside the Saraste dimer interface, and IP6 does not participate in any interactions between the two Btk subunits in that dimer.
source: The mechanism of IP6-induced transient Btk dimerization is fundamentally different, in that the peripheral IP6 binding site is just outside the Saraste dimer interface, and IP6 does not participate in any interactions between the two Btk subunits in that dimer.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the structural mechanisms.

claim: Fusion of a Btk PH-TH module with the catalytic domain of another kinase that autophosphorylates slowly should impart activation by IP6 if the effect of IP6 arises from its ability to promote dimerization of the PH-TH module.
source: If the effect of IP6 arises from its ability to promote dimerization of the PH-TH module, fusion of a Btk PH-TH module with the catalytic domain of another kinase that autophosphorylates slowly should impart activation by IP6.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to be tested experimentally.

claim: c-Abl is a good example of a kinase that autophosphorylates slowly.
source: A good example of such a kinase is c-Abl.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In chronic myelogenous leukemia, a chromosomal translocation results in fusion of a coiled-coil oligomerization domain with c-Abl, leading to hyper-activation of the BCR-Abl fusion protein by autophosphorylation.
source: Indeed, in chronic myelogenous leukemia, a chromosomal translocation results in fusion of a coiled-coil oligomerization domain with c-Abl, leading to hyper-activation of the BCR-Abl fusion protein by autophosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about BCR-Abl.

claim: Several other fusion variants involving c-Abl, in which different oligomerization domains are present, are associated with hematological malignancies.
source: Several other fusion variants involving c-Abl, in which different oligomerization domains are present, are associated with hematological malignancies (De Braekeleer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The PH-TH-Abl fusion protein at a concentration of 1 μM autophosphorylated slowly in the absence of IP6, while the IP6-bound protein became heavily phosphorylated within the first 30 s.
source: The fusion protein at a concentration of 1 μM autophosphorylated slowly in the absence of IP6, while the IP6-bound protein became heavily phosphorylated within the first 30 s, the dead-time of our assay (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: The autophosphorylation rate of the PH-TH-Abl mutant (Y42R/F44R) in the presence of IP6 was much lower than that of the IP6-bound wild-type protein.
source: We replaced Phe 44 and Tyr 42, at the Saraste dimer interface, with arginine in the fusion protein. The autophosphorylation rate of the PH-TH-Abl mutant in the presence of IP6 was much lower than that of the IP6-bound wild-type protein, further evidence for the importance of the Saraste dimer interface in IP6-mediated activation (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: The Btk and c-Abl kinase domains are 46% identical in sequence, but most of the surface residues are different.
source: The Btk and c-Abl kinase domains are 46% identical in sequence, but most of the surface residues are different.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Except for its enzymatic activity, the interaction properties of the Btk kinase domain are not important for the IP6 response.
source: We infer that, except for its enzymatic activity, the interaction properties of the Btk kinase domain are not important for the IP6 response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PH-TH-Abl fusion data.

claim: IP6 promotes transphosphorylation of the attached kinase by inducing transient dimerization when kinases are linked to the Btk PH-TH module.
source: Because IP6 activates both kinases when they are linked to the Btk PH-TH module, we propose that IP6 promotes transphosphorylation of the attached kinase by inducing transient dimerization.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data.

claim: The IP6-induced dimerization of the Btk PH-TH module is very weak, with a dissociation constant that is likely to be greater than 100 μM.
source: Our preliminary studies indicate that the IP6-induced dimerization of the Btk PH-TH module is very weak, with a dissociation constant that is likely to be greater than 100 μM.
evidence: This is based on preliminary biophysical studies.

claim: Even a modest increase in a small dimer population can lead to a sharp change in the rate of activation because the reaction is autocatalytic.
source: A simple calculation shows that even a modest increase in a small dimer population can lead to a sharp change in the rate of activation because the reaction is autocatalytic.
evidence: This is based on kinetic modeling calculations.

claim: The failure to detect stable dimers of the Btk PH-TH module or of full-length Btk in the presence of IP6 suggests that the monomeric PH-TH module has a conformation different from the one seen in crystal structures.
source: Our failure to detect stable dimers of the Btk PH-TH module or of full-length Btk in the presence of IP6 suggests that the monomeric PH-TH module has a conformation different from the one seen in crystal structures, which all show the same dimer contact.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biophysical data and crystal structures.

claim: The high protein concentration in the crystal lattice (∼30 mM) presumably drives the formation of the Saraste dimer, which is otherwise not favored.
source: The high protein concentration in the crystal lattice (∼30 mM) presumably drives the formation of the Saraste dimer, which is otherwise not favored.
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystallographic and solution data.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that the conformation of the PH-TH module seen in the Saraste dimer is unstable when the protein is monomeric.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that the conformation of the PH-TH module seen in the Saraste dimer is unstable when the protein is monomeric.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Within the first 30 ns of simulation of monomeric PH-TH, the β3-β4 hairpin bent towards the core of the PH-TH module.
source: Within the first 30 ns of simulation, the β3-β4 hairpin bent towards the core of the PH-TH module (Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A), and Phe 44, at the heart of the Saraste dimer interface, changed its conformation and packed against the other three interfacial residues, Tyr 42, Ile 9, and IIe 95 (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The conformational change in the PH-TH module during simulation closed the dimer interface, burying the interfacial residues.
source: This conformational change closed the dimer interface, burying the interfacial residues.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The hydrophobicity of the dimer interface drove the observed conformational change in the PH-TH module during simulation.
source: The hydrophobicity of the dimer interface drove the observed conformational change.
evidence: This is an inference based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations initiated from crystal structures but with the four interfacial residues substituted by alanine reduced the extent of conformational change in the dimer interface area.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations initiated from crystal structures but with the four interfacial residues substituted by alanine reduced the extent of conformational change in this area (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The peripheral binding site for IP6 is adjacent to the β3-β4 hairpin that folds in and closes the dimer interface in the simulation.
source: The peripheral binding site for IP6 is adjacent to the β3-β4 hairpin that folds in and closes the dimer interface in the simulation.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: One effect of IP6 binding may be to stabilize the open form of the β3-β4 hairpin.
source: Thus, one effect of IP6 binding may be to stabilize the open form of the hairpin.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the structural and simulation data.

claim: The PH-TH domain carries seven net positive charges and is electrostatically polarized, with the positively charged residues concentrated on a broad, contiguous surface.
source: The PH-TH domain carries seven net positive charges; it is also electrostatically polarized, with the positively charged residues concentrated on the broad, contiguous surface composed of the β3-β4 hairpin, the IP4 binding loop and the N-terminal region of the loop connecting strand β5 and helix α2.
evidence: This is based on electrostatic calculations.

claim: In the Saraste dimer, positive electrostatic field lines calculated based on the monomer run into each other at the dimer interface, suggesting that electrostatic forces oppose dimer formation.
source: In the Saraste dimer, positive electrostatic field lines calculated based on the monomer run into each other at the dimer interface, suggesting that electrostatic forces oppose dimer formation.
evidence: This is based on electrostatic calculations and is a reasonable inference.

claim: The autophosphorylation rate of full-length Btk with the K49E/R52E mutations was substantially higher than that of the wild-type protein, with pronounced phosphorylation observed in the first 2 min of the reaction.
source: We introduced two charge-reversal mutations at the peripheral IP6-binding site (K49E and R52E), to reduce the positive charge on the protein by four units. The autophosphorylation rate of full-length Btk with the K49E/R52E mutations was substantially higher than that of the wild-type protein, with pronounced phosphorylation observed in the first 2 min of the reaction (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: There are two barriers to the dimerization of the PH-TH module of Btk: the dimer interface is probably closed in the monomeric protein, and an electrostatic repulsion between PH domains further impedes dimerization.
source: We suggest that there are two barriers to the dimerization of the PH-TH module of Btk. First, the dimer interface of the PH domain is probably closed in the monomeric protein. Second, an electrostatic repulsion between PH domains further impedes dimerization.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the structural, simulation, and biochemical data.

claim: IP6 binding might stabilize the open form of the PH-TH module allosterically, while also alleviating the electrostatic repulsion.
source: IP6 binding might stabilize the open form of the PH-TH module allosterically, while also alleviating the electrostatic repulsion.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the data.

claim: The Src-like module of Btk adopts a compact and autoinhibited form that resembles the autoinhibited structures of the Src kinases and c-Abl, in which the SH3 domain binds to the SH2-kinase linker and holds the kinase domain in an inactive conformation.
source: Our studies on Btk have revealed the structural basis for its autoinhibition. One key finding is that the Src-like module of Btk adopts a compact and autoinhibited form that resembles the autoinhibited structures of the Src kinases and c-Abl, in which the SH3 domain binds to the SH2-kinase linker and holds the kinase domain in an inactive conformation.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings.

claim: The structure of the PH-TH-kinase construct of Btk shows that the PH-TH module stabilizes the inactive conformation of the kinase domain, as well as the assembled conformation of the Src-like module of Btk.
source: Our structure of the PH-TH-kinase construct of Btk shows that the PH-TH module stablizes the inactive conformation of the kinase domain, as well as the assembled conformation of the Src-like module of Btk.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings.

claim: IP6 can activate Btk strongly by binding to a newly identified site on the PH domain, probably by promoting transient dimerization of the PH-TH module.
source: A second, and quite unexpected, finding is that IP6 can activate Btk strongly by binding to a newly identified site on the PH domain, probably by promoting transient dimerization of the PH-TH module.
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings.

claim: Because IP6 synthesis requires the precursor molecule IP3, which is itself produced as a result of Btk activation, a transient elevation of IP6 may create a positive feedback loop for Btk activation, either on the membrane or in the cytoplasm.
source: Because IP6 synthesis requires the precursor molecule IP3, which is itself produced as a result of Btk activation, a transient elevation of IP6 may create a positive feedback loop for Btk activation, either on the membrane or in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings and knowledge of IP6 metabolism.

claim: Formation of the Saraste dimer interface is compatible with the simultaneous engagement of PIP3 by both PH domains in the dimer, raising the possibility that IP6 can stimulate dimerization of membrane-tethered Btk.
source: Formation of the Saraste dimer interface is compatible with the simultaneous engagement of PIP3 by both PH domains in the dimer, raising the possibility that IP6 can stimulate dimerization of membrane-tethered Btk (Figure 10).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on structural analysis.

claim: IP6 binding to the peripheral binding site may also enhance PIP3 affinity in the canonical binding site and sensitize Btk to PIP3 levels.
source: IP6 binding to the peripheral binding site may also enhance PIP3 affinity in the canonical binding site and sensitize Btk to PIP3 levels.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning.

claim: The linker connecting the PH-TH unit to the SH3 domain promotes dimerization of Btk by interacting with the SH3 domain of a second molecule, providing an additional mechanism for Btk dimerization at high local concentration.
source: The linker connecting the PH-TH unit to the SH3 domain promotes dimerization of Btk by interacting with the SH3 domain of a second molecule, providing an additional mechanism for Btk dimerization at high local concentration (Laederach et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: High levels of IP6 may down-regulate the amount of Btk on membranes by competing for PIP3 binding in the canonical binding site, as proposed for Akt1 regulation by IP7.
source: High levels of IP6 may down-regulate the amount of Btk on membranes by competing for PIP3 binding in the canonical binding site, as proposed for Akt1 regulation by IP7 (Chakraborty et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on analogy to Akt1, supported by citation.

claim: The Src-like modules of Btk and Itk have 55% sequence identity, with all the residues critical for maintaining the assembled and autoinhibited Src-like conformation of Btk conserved in Itk.
source: The Src-like modules of Btk and Itk have 55% sequence identity, with all the residues critical for maintaining the assembled and autoinhibited Src-like conformation of Btk conserved in Itk (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment.

claim: The Src-like module of Itk is therefore likely also to adopt the assembled Src-like conformation when inactive.
